title: Gas Holder

introduction.definition: A wet gas holder stores low-pressure gas in a steel bell floating in a water tank. As gas flows in the bell rises; as gas is drawn off it sinks. The water forms the seal and the bell's weight keeps the pressure nearly constant.
key_points: Modern sites use dry membrane holders
introduction.summary: A wet gas holder stores low-pressure gas (biogas, town gas, process gas) in a steel bell that floats in a water-filled tank. As gas comes in, the bell rises; as gas is drawn off, it sinks. The water forms the seal and the bell's weight sets a nearly constant gas pressure.

video_tutorials.title: Gas Holder — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Gas Holder.
A wet gas holder stores low-pressure gas in a steel bell floating in a water tank.
As gas flows in the bell rises; as gas is drawn off it sinks.
The water forms the seal and the bell's weight keeps the pressure nearly constant.
Typical applications include biogas plants (wet/dry holders); historic town-gas storage; process gas buffering; landfill gas balancing.
The cutaway reveals the internal construction.
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.
Next, watch the operation tutorial to see how it works.

video_tutorials.title: Gas Holder — Operation

script.narration: How the Gas Holder works.
Gas enters through the inlet pipe rising through the water.
The bell lifts as the gas volume increases.
The guide frame and rollers keep it vertical.
When gas is drawn off, the bell sinks under its own weight.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.

video_tutorials.title: Gas Holder — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Gas Holder.
Check bell level and water seal.
Inspect rollers and guides.
Repaint bell and tank.
Watch for bell jamming: tilting, pressure surges. Common cause: roller/guide wear, ice.
Watch for water seal loss: gas leak. Common cause: evaporation, leak.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
